utterances.text: Are you asking me? Yes, generally speaking, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now let me just read one more sentence, which says: "I'm not sure who of my colleagues approached me and offered me his hand. After that, I stood up. At that moment, I realised that I almost cannot see anything with my right eye." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: Yes, only later on I gave the name of the person who helped me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't mention this person. You refer to it as a male, but this is not so relevant. Let me continue with my questions about the statement presented to you by my colleague Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: Am I allowed to ask any questions or make statements?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, just answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please display document 65 ter 02994, tendered as Prosecutor's evidence 295. Let us look at page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at paragraph 9, the last paragraph in the B/C/S version, and it says: "I could not see very well and tried to wipe my eyes. I then realised that my eyes and face were covered in blood." Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you never mention any blood at the time when you gave your first statement immediately after the incident, but you rather said what I read to you a while ago, that you almost couldn't see anything with your right eye and you never mentioned any blood. How do you account for that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: How do I account for that? As far as I remember, very soon after the explosion and the injuries, the police sought statements; and if my memory serves me well, I most probably said that. I don't know what they -- why they didn't record it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay, I understand. You did change slightly your statement regarding the shrapnel embedded in your right cheek; and in paragraph 12 of this same statement, you say as follows. "The material was embedded in my skin and started emerging or getting out a few weeks later." Is that how it happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: In the bag and in the front part of my body, after I would get up in the morning, I would find pieces getting out of my body. My skin was sore, and these were pieces of dirt and glass.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please display now for the benefit of the Chamber, 65 ter 00185A already tendered -- shown by the Prosecution, and that's the medical record that we have already seen. There, that's the document. I don't see the English yet. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It says: "Clinic for Eye Diseases, Sarajevo, date 17 July 1995;" and then it says what occurred on the 28th: "On the 28th of June, 1995, Rialda Musaefendic was admitted to the outpatient clinic on account of conjunctivitis traumatica. Is this the only document that you have left that after all of this, everything we have heard about, everything that you went through at the time? Is this the only document that you still have? Is this the only document to show that you had shards of glass embedded in your skin, everything you told us about? Or is it only about this conjunctivitis, which every second person on this planet probably suffers from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: Nobody asked me to provide a single finding. I should perhaps put them altogether and then bring them. During the war, people went to hospitals to receive treatment, but nobody really cared about the paperwork to be frank.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to go back to the statement dated the 11th of March, 1997. I have to go back to that statement in order to show the witness something else, which is 65 ter 02 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not a doctor; but if my learned friend is trying to indicate that the witness suffered from conjunctivitis, which -- which is in my submission distinct to conjunctivitis traumatica, I believe the word "trauma" has some significance in this medical record, and it's simply not just conjunctivitis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you have contradicted yourself. Apparently you have some learning in the matter to do. Mr. Tapuskovic, what are you trying to suggest by this line of questioning? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just ask an additional question about this document, then I'll tell you. Because in this statement the witness claims that a piece of shrapnel hit her right sinus and the area above her right eye. So that's another allegation that she makes in the next statement and I can show you that. It's precisely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that her story, her evidence is a fabrication?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me hear the rest of your questioning to see the extent of which you are able to substantiate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will first ask the Witness this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about CNN? They were on the spot on that day, weren't they? Did they take any statements from the people there, statements like this? Did they not show this as one of the most serious crimes committed by the Serb side; isn't that right. This whole wide world saw this incident, and this was presented as something as committed by the Serb side; including what you described in this statement. Isn't that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Do you mean that particular day, because that day I was in the hospital. Once I was back, of course, I went back to my home to see my mother. I'm not sure what you're asking me about, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about the world propaganda? Did the world propaganda not seize on this and use it to present as a crime committed by the Serbs, what Mr. Silajdzic said a while ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: As far as I know, the TV crews and the TV agencies filmed the truth and nothing but the truth which is what they always do, isn't it? And they simply broadcast their coverage throughout the world. That's as much as I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you at least allow for the possibility that it was the BH army targeting the TV building in order to then show this up as something, a crime, perhaps, committed by the other side? Is this a possibility that you found -- you find plausible at least?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: What exactly are you asking me? Can I just ask you, I'm not sure I understand your question. What exactly do you want me to confirm? Yes, no? What sort of answer are you expecting?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In this case, or in any other case for that matter, is it possible that the BH army targeted their own people in order to present this to the world as a crime committed by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know about this incident either, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: About this incident, I know where the shell came from, I know where the bomb came from, because that was the safest part of the TV building. The second floor, inside the atrium, it was the safest place in the TV building. Frankly, I don't what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just in order to assist the Chamber, where did the bomb come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: It landed on the roof. It slid right down and eventually exploded inside the atrium. That's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And who fired the bomb on the TV building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: From that side of the roof, facing that side of the roof is Ilidza, as far as I know, and throughout the war this area was being held by the army of Republika Srpska and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that there were international observers there, monitors - and I'm not showing you any of that - who claimed that this particular missile had been fired by the BH army, from territory held by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: First I hear of it. I'd like to hear them confirm it for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The OTP never showed you any of those, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: No. Are they supposed to? I don't know. I'm not privy to this, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I, for one, believe that they should have shown you that particular document, a document that clearly indicates, which is far from saying it's the absolute truth. It's for the Chamber to judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, that is out of order. That is a comment. Speaking for myself, there are two issues in this case, Mr. Tapuskovic and the Defence. The first issue is from what direction did the bombs or the shells come, from whose side? Did they come from the side of the Serbs or from the side of the Bosnian government, the Muslims? That's the first issue and the main issue. The second issue is the responsibility of the accused under Article 7(3), command responsibility. We haven't yet touched on that. But the first one that I've identified is, in my view, speaking for myself, the issue on which the Defence should be concentrating. I don't see how it advances the case of the Defence for you to suggest that this witness did not suffer the injuries that she alleges. How does that advance your case? Your questioning should be directed at showing that the bombs did not come from the side of the Serbs. That's the issue in this case: Where did the bombs come from? Not trying to suggest that she's not speaking the truth about the injuries that she suffered. That doesn't seem to make much sense to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will never deny any of the human suffering suffered by the victims, but each witness has to establish some sort of credibility in order for to us be able to take their words at face value. I never, for a moment, doubt it, nor will I ever for a moment try to deny anybody's suffering. Look at paragraph 27, for example. Her statement, the very last paragraph, the 17th of May. It's the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's look at it when we resume. We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You were directing us to paragraph 27 of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true. I will get to it eventually. But I do have a sequence of my own to follow, and I won't take long, I promise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Follow your own sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the 65 ter statement 00185, the one that I dealt with earlier on. This is page 85 in e-court. Can that please be admitted as a Defence exhibit, the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe there's no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it that we are to admit? It's not the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's her statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the statement, the first statement, that I questioned the witness on; the 19th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be admitted as Exhibit D92.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would like you to clarify paragraph 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can 65 ter 0294 be brought up for the benefit of the witness. This is OTP Exhibit 259, a statement dated the 17th of May. Paragraph 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that, Witness? Here's my question: You say: "There were Serb snipers in the hills above Hrasno and also in the Grbavica stadium, and a favourite target of theirs was the street adjacent to our building known as Ive Kranjecevica Street and now known as Dzamijska Street. The Serb forces were at the foot of the hill." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to see because the print is so small. I find it difficult to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it better now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So I won't read it again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that. Paragraph 21. The Serb snipers and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. "In the hills above Hrasno," what does that mean? Which hill is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: Above Hrasno there is Hrasno Brdo. That's what it's called, Hrasno hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And who was holding these positions, the main elevations on the top of Hrasno hill at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "main elevations." I know that the streets bordering on the Zeljeznicar stadium lead in the direction of Hrasno hill, and those streets were under the control of the army of Republika Srpska and the JNA at the time. If you were a Muslim, it just wasn't possible to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about between the 10th of August, 1994, and the 21st of November, 1995. That's the time period I'm asking about you. What sort of JNA are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: The period that you have just specified, I suppose that includes as the terminal date the date that the Dayton Accords were signed. I'm not sure which period you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Everything I'm asking about is about this time-period, the time-period between the 10th of August, 1994, and the 21st of November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: Yes. There was firing there. They were still up there. There were wounded people all around. You still couldn't cross those streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So please explain this -- very well, okay. But what about this: The Serb forces were at the foot of the hill. So who was up on the hill and who was at the foot of the hill? Can you explain the distinction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: I'll do my best. There's this area that we call Zeljo's stadium, the football pitch belonging to FC Zeljeznicar. That's at the foot of the hill. And then there is Hrasno hill. The stadium connects Pero Kosoric Square and the neighbourhood of Grbavica. That's at the foot of the hill and Hrasno Brdo is on the top of the hill, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So who is holding the positions on top of Hrasno hill? Which army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: At the time that you specified, along the top of the hill, there were Serb soldiers, the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And then further down you say: "We were near the front lines." What are you trying to say there? What exactly were these front lines like in that area of Sarajevo, Hrasno?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: Hrasno, all right, I can tell you about my neighbourhood, where I lived. There was just a single street between us and the front line, so that was the front line, a single street. There's a trolley-bus running along that street now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would the front line sometimes not cut across houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I mean one part of the house on one side of the front and the other on the other side of the front.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: That certainly didn't apply to my neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Anyway, you are stating categorically that on top of Hrasno hill there was the army of Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: Yes, on top of the hill and at the Zeljo's stadium, as I said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But isn't Zeljo's stadium down at the foot of the hill, in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, you asked me to repeat and to tell you exactly what I meant here, "at the foot of the hill." I explained what I meant by "at the foot of the hill." There's a stadium right there, and these guys were on top of the hill. I thought that explained it sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I want to make this clear for the benefit of the Chamber. Both Grbavica and Hrasno Brdo were being held by the army of Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: Yes, the top of Hrasno hill and Grbavica as well; that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to wrap this up. There's not that much left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 27, which is the last paragraph, the last paragraph of this statement. Paragraph 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If my understanding is correct, you did a bit of journalism, too. You worked with this American agency, didn't you, at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: It's only been brought up now, 27. I started working with the agency. Well, you know, this is the usual practice whenever you come to an agency: First I brewed coffee for people and then I became the assistant producer and then producer and then the office manager. I was moving up and my title, my job title, changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about the time that I discussed a while ago, the end of 1994 and November 1995? You were well informed about everything that was happening in Sarajevo, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean, "well informed"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you knew what was happening in that final year, for example, who was firing at whom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: If you are seeking my opinion, yes, I did know who was shooting and I knew where I was living.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to me -- you mentioned an aggressor several times earlier. Can you explain to me what do you mean by an aggressor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: An aggressor, in my view, is someone who allows me one day to lead a normal life, and then on the next day or two days later there was mortar shell and my first neighbour loses a finger and then suddenly there is war. That's what I call aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: Aggression against me personally and the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what's happening about the people on the other side of the front?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: I don't understand. Where you are referring to? I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 27, you say: "I experienced a degree of sadness when the peace agreement was signed and the war was over, because I realised that this could have been done achieved much earlier and would have saved a lot of the lives." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about who, in 1993, didn't want peace at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: What do you mean? Who didn't want to conclude a peace agreement at all? I know that I personally didn't want war to happen at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody wanted the war. There is not a sane and reasonable person in the country who wanted war. But I'm asking you, do you know anything, since you worked for the new agency, who was against this agreement which would provide for avoiding further victims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: I only know who continued shelling Sarajevo and that was the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question and then I'll conclude my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I need to tender the document, 65 ter 02995, dated 11th of March, 1997. That's the statement given by Witness Rialda. And if we can have it brought up on the screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you seeking to tender this, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let me just show a small portion of it to the witness, and after that, I will move for it to be admitted. I will be very brief. I just actually want to ask one question in relation to this document, page 2, paragraph 5. I think it won't be difficult to find it both in the English and B/C/S versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to what you said with regard to this conjunctivitis you mentioned, and when you said there was no other paper relating to your injuries. You said that: "I received a shrapnel wound to my right sinus and above my left eye. I had small bits of metal in my face and lots of cuts on my back and other parts of my body." That's your last statement, and is it true, that you said this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: If it's reads like that, then it is. I would only like to say that initially I asked for an explanation for this. I know exactly what I went through, and I know that I was wounded by a piece of metal, by pieces of reinforced concrete and bars. And I think I said that at the beginning. As far as medical records are concerned, I said that nobody asked me to provide them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have corrected your statement with regard to what you said on the 17th of May, but this is a completely different thing. What I read out to you is something completely different. And you stand by this, that this is how it happened and this is what you went through?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-50
utterances.text: I stand by the fact that I survived a modified aerial bomb which landed on the 28th of June, 1995, on the TV building of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that I had experienced trauma.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave -- and I will finish with this. By your leave, I would like to present a document that I referred to on several occasions. It's D31, marked for identification through this witness. I would like to tender it, but first of all, let me just say one very fundamental thing. There is an UNPROFOR report showing that, according to UNPROFOR and their findings, the TV building was fired on by the BH army. Can the witness comment on this. It's our number DD00-0463.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. Well, now the document is on the screen, but I would just ask counsel to be accurate in the way he presents the contents of this document. It's a report and it reports on another person stating that he had heard or he had seen and, according to him -- in other words, a report filed by somebody else that this was fired by the BH army. It's not, in my submission, a conclusion or a definite fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you: Witness, do you know anything about an UNPROFOR report to the effect that -- it's from a Captain Hansen, Captain Hansen, who is reporting something that was told to him to the effect that the TV building had been fired on by the BH army? First, do you know anything about that report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what do you say to the suggestion that the TV building was fired upon by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the BH army did not fire upon the TV building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have any specific grounds for that belief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, in terms that I'm capable of providing you with evidence. But no, in the condition of the BH army, especially in Sarajevo, how they were organised and other things, they were defending their lives; and in addition to that, they didn't have that type of weapons. And prior to that I never heard of these type of weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. She can't help any further with this document, Mr. Tapuskovic. In any event, this document has been marked for identification, and you'll recall that I have invited the Prosecution to call Mr. Hansen, Captain Hansen, rather, and I will get a report from the Prosecution early next week. If I'm not satisfied with the report, the Chamber will call Captain Hansen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm going to finalise now, but I asked your permission to ask the witness about this, and I said that at the very outset. But I don't understand Mr. Sachdeva's attitude, that this is just a story rather than an official UNPROFOR report, something that has been highly regarded by this Court. That's all I wanted to say, and with this I conclude my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, do you want me to respond to this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. He has completed his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: No. No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your evidence is now completed; we thank you for giving it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't ask that this last statement be tendered into evidence; 65 ter 02995, dated the 11th of March. I just showed the witness a small portion thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It seems as if you have tendered it. It's D93. I will just ask the court deputy to confirm.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, it's admitted as D93.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Waespi is taking the next witness. Might I be excused for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness is Dzemaludin Luinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please sit. And you may begin, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If 65 ter number 02996, a witness statement dated the 10th of March, 1997, could be retrieved, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Dzemaludin Luinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please look at the document which appears on your screen. Please let us know if you cannot read properly because it's too small. Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: I recognise my signature, but I cannot read. I left my glasses in Sarajevo, so it's going to be difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thanks for letting us know. I hope we can do without your glasses. I hope. But can you go as far as saying this is the witness statement you gave to investigators from the Tribunal on the 10th of March, 1997?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you have a chance to review this statement this morning in my office? And I think that parts of it were read out to you; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the second page of this document, to the third paragraph, the last line - and I can read it for you - it talks about you being --

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The paragraph talks about you being a reserve policeman in Sarajevo, starting from 15 May 1995 until 1996. And then, and I quote: "During the period of the war, my private workshop was also used as a workshop for the BH army." That private workshop is, as you see from the previous paragraph, a shop repairing car bodies on a private basis. Now, is it true that you also worked for the BH army, or was it, rather, somebody else?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Please, I'll tell you the truth. This was my workshop before the war, but I allowed the Novi Grad police station to use it because I was a member of the reserve police force. As long as I had material, I was able to work on mostly small cars, Golf cars. When I ran out of material, they took me to work as a policeman securing various facilities, streets, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Luinovic, for this clarification. Now, with this correction, is the witness statement, as you read it this morning in my office, a true and accurate record of what you told the investigator about your experience in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if you were to answer the same questions today, would these answers be the same as recorded in your statement of 10 March 1997?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: I have nothing to change. What I saw I will describe, and what I suffered I also described.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Luinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to tender this statement, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P297, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If a second document could be retrieved. It's ter number 02997, a second witness statement the witness gave to the Office of the Prosecutor. If the document on the left could be scrolled to the bottom so the signature blocks are seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Luinovic, is that a second witness statement you gave to the investigators of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is my signature and I corroborate that. Probably it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Are you sure it is, or is it only probable?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: This is my statement; this is my signature; therefore ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to read your statement, or, rather, was it read out to you this morning in my office?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: It was read out to me in full. There was just a minor correction, and we saw what it was all about a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in relation to this second document, which dates last year, 26th of April, 2006, if you were to answer the same questions today, would these answers be the same as recorded in this statement?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Although it's been many years now, I think that this statement and the one I gave a few years ago would coincide at least 90 per cent or perhaps even 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Luinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if that could be tendered as an exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P298, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I do have only one additional exhibit with this witness, and that's a photo, ter number 02998. If that could be retrieved, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And while that is being done, Mr. Luinovic, I do have a few questions for you but it shouldn't take too long. Do you remember the 26th of May, 1995, when your neighbourhood was shelled? Do you remember that day?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, clearly, as if I'm looking at it right now. On the 26th of May, 1995, of course I was a member of the reserve police. Upon arrival at the police station on that day, I was given my assignment, an order to go to Novi Grad municipality in Sarajevo. I went to Novi Grad municipality and I provided security for the municipality building. That was an eight-hour shift. I was a bit tired after working on the beat around the building; I just leaned against it. And it must have been -- I never measured it, but it must have been 5 kilometres, as the crow flies, to Ilidza. While I was resting a bit, I saw something big coming from Ilidza, and as it was coming closer and closer, I thought that it was an airplane. And I said to myself, It's impossible that an airplane is flying so low. It's going to hit one of these buildings here for sure." Just a few seconds later, it hit a building next to the house, my house, because my house is just opposite. Between 20 and 25 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Luinovic, thus far. Can we have a look at the photo which should be displayed on your screen. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see that. I see it clearly. It's been long since I last looked at a photograph like this. I've never seen my neighbourhood photographed this way. I recognise every blade of grass.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: I can show you my home, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, please, with the assistance of Mr. Usher, if you could take one of these magic pens and mark your home, please.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: This is my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: This is my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you add the letter A, please, next to it.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: The building that the shell landed on?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No. First, just next to the circle, where you have indicated where your home was.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you add the letter A?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. And then can you indicate where the municipal building was, where you were standing as a guard that morning?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: The municipal hall -- it's like this. It's from this intersection and then this way. This is the transformer building, the high-voltage building, the transformer, the electricity, you know. It's right next to the municipal hall, so it should be around here. It's right here. This is the waterworks building, this building over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: It's water for drinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You made several markings now. Can you please indicate with the letter B where you say that the municipal building was.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: The municipal hall. It didn't catch on. I don't have it in the photograph, you know, but it's this way, and then this goes all the way towards the municipal building. Letter D, there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. So you marked -- just on top of that four-lane road, you marked a few circles, concentrated circles, and that's the direction you say the municipal building was.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us, in metres, how far away was the municipal building from your home, which you have indicated with the letter A? What was the distance, if you can tell?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really measure it, so this is more like debt reckoning. You probably would need a land surveyor there to give you the distance. But what I would say, just by looking at it, 250 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Luinovic. Now, when you were on guard, on duty, rather, outside the municipal building, did you wear a uniform; were you armed?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: I was wearing a uniform, a camouflage uniform. I was carrying a semi-automatic rifle, a pistol, and a truncheon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Luinovic. Now, going back to that projectile you saw coming from Ilidza, how far away were you from the projectile? I guess it's very difficult to judge that, but do you have an opinion how far away you were from that projectile when you saw it for the first time?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: The first time I saw it, I think it was about 2 kilometres from where I was standing, which means 2.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you see where it was landing?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you indicate on this photo where it was landing.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you add the letter C next to this last mark.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, this projectile, do you know what kind of projectile it was? Was it a mortar? Was it an artillery grenade? Was it something else?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: This was a rocket shell fired from a launching pad. It couldn't have been done by an artillery weapon or anything like that. How shall I put it? I'm really no military expert at all, but I do know a thing or two. It's a big mortar shell and you need a launching pad for something like that. I suppose the JNA had those. Not that I saw any; just an assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said a moment ago you saw the impact. Can you describe that, the impact, as you saw it?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. I saw it coming from up there. I thought it was a plane flying low, or something like that, about to hit the ground. And then it hit this building. It wasn't before then that I realised that this was a shell with the two or three motors. I really hadn't a clue. I'm no military analyst or anything. But it probably had some motors, a system in place for propulsion. So it's the same sort of distance at which another couple of shells landed which I hadn't seen coming. But I did see this one and I can tell about this. As for those other ones, those other shells, I can't say because I didn't see them coming in. When I realised that the shell hit this building and it was near my home - it's the building next to my home - there was so much dust in the air and bits of concrete flying all over the place; mortar off the walls; doors and windows smashed; bits flying through the air. There was rubble strewn all across the road. So I ran and I ran from here, in this direction. I was reckoning, I was hoping that none of my family had been killed. It was so difficult to see. The dust was so thick that I couldn't even see the building. There was so much dust flying. When I realised that the shell had hit the building, I went to the other building, to my home. My daughter was out in the yard; she was crying. I took her in my arms and I took her to our neighbour's house. I stayed in my own front yard with my father, watching. I realised that they weren't bringing out any body. Two or three cars arrived. UNPROFOR, UNHCR. I hadn't a clue, to be frank, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Elicit the evidence bit by bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You mentioned, Mr. Luinovic, that there were, apart from this specific projectile, other shells that landed near your home. Can you tell us exactly where these other shells landed.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Sure, of course. I told my father immediately, "I know what they're doing. They're firing a large shell and then they're firing more small shells to hurt more people." Many people were killed in Sarajevo because they went out to see where the shells had fallen, which resulted in more casualties than strictly necessary. And I told my father, "Listen, old man, go back to your home and I'll go back to mine until the whole thing settles down." I took my daughter and I took her to my neighbour's basement. I went back to my own house, to the bathroom to be more precise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question that was asked was: Can you tell us exactly where these other shells landed? Where did the shells land?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first shell that landed? Can I mark it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: There. It fell right there. It came from Ilidza. It hit the tarmac right here, the road. I mean it ricochetted and smashed against my building, drilling a two-by-two hole.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Luinovic. Now, you just made a marking between letter A and C in the middle of that four-lane road. Can you please add the letter D to that last marking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, on several occasions the witness has said that the shell came from Ilidza. Could he tell us and show us on this photograph where the shell came from, from Ilidza? Could we see this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Sure, sure. I'm looking at it. This is the shell that came from Ilidza, right here, and from Ilidza, right here. And Ilidza is over there, roughly speaking, you see. And then further up there's another --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Luinovic, it's very difficult for us to follow you unless it is recorded, what are you doing on the photo. Can you tell us -- you made a few marks originating from the letter C towards the left. Do these marks indicate where you say the direction of these shells, where they were flying in?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Luinovic. So you're saying that Ilidza is on the left side of this photo or on the right side of this photo?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: To the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Luinovic. Now, let me ask you just a couple of more things. Looking at this photo, were there any military targets in this area, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I am against military targets in this area. You see this neighbourhood? They would have wiped us all out. They would have wiped us all out. There was no military formation there, just civilians, people who had been mobilised. Some drafted into the army, some into the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, on this morning were there any soldiers walking around, running around, you know, assembling together, according to what you saw and observed when you were on duty on -- near that municipality building?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice anyone, really, no one moving about. Maybe some headed for their shifts, on their way to work. They all had shifts. But there was nothing like that. You know, even three or four people assembling, you know, you would hear things like that. You heard shells falling all over the place. You weren't supposed to be caught outside, were you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: My last question is, in 1994 and 1995, did you ever see a mortar or any other weaponry operated by the ABiH forces in this area, this area you see on this photo?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: I never went to the front line. I was living my life on Sarajevo's asphalt all the time. I don't even know. I had my own rifle. It was so rusty that I passed it on to someone to clean it for me, because rain would fall and then the iron bits. I never really cleaned it properly myself. I gave it to someone else to clean. But I never fired a single bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just reiterate my question. Did you see ABiH mortars being located, being fired, being stationed, anywhere in this neighbourhood, the one we see here in this photo? Can you answer that question, please.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. No, no, no. Not here. Not here. No military formations at all, not around this neighbourhood. I'm not say other places. But this neighbourhood, my neighbourhood, no military there. No necessity either. What we would have had soldiers there for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps you can explain that, when you say, "What would we have had soldiers there for?" Are you suggesting that there would have been no need for ABiH soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a town. The front lines were outside the town, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where would one find the nearest set of ABiH soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Far away; 3 kilometres, 4, perhaps, from this neighbourhood. No nearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 3 to 4 kilometres. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And in what direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In what direction would one find those ABiH soldiers, 3 to 4 kilometres away? Perhaps even more precisely, can you tell us where that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me tell you one thing. There was this belt around Sarajevo. The front line was around Sarajevo. There was no front line inside Sarajevo. That's where the city was. You defend a city outside the city, around the city, not inside. If we had allowed the Serbs to get in, they would have slit all of our throats. But I'm telling you, we guarded our town from outside, from around it. I never went to the front line because I was some sort of a policeman, that sort of thing. I was securing buildings; I was walking the beat, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question. How far were the Serb lines from the army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, from where my home was, I would say that the nearest line was at Nedzarici, 4.5 kilometres, perhaps 5 kilometres from my home. It's difficult to say, but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And perhaps to conclude, for everybody's understanding of this photo, I see a couple of significant buildings on this photo. The one on top, the large one, kind of yellowish, can you tell Their Honours what that building was.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: You mean this one to the right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No. If you look at this dotted line you made, indicating the direction where the shells were coming from Ilidza just above it, you kind of see a large building.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please mark it with a circle.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Please add the letter E next to it.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Luinovic. What was that building in May --

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: This was a school. This was a school. You see no windows on it, no doors. People took it away to use as firewood because they needed to cook their meals. As for the rest, this was for small children, like a creche, daycare.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next building I'm interested in is at the bottom. At the very bottom we have private homes, it appears, and just above them there are a couple of flat buildings, bottom left. Can you tell Their Honours what these buildings were used for during the war?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: This building right here. The low building right here, you see a single floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Can you make a circle around it again.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: It's like this. Let's do it like this, because you might want to know about this other building, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Can you add the letter F, please.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: F?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. It looks like an F to me. Can you please explain what the building was used for.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: This building is still used -- it was just like it was in wartime. This is the heating plant. This is where they kept the coals, you know, small bits of coal used for heating. Are you interested in any other buildings?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The building just below that heating plant.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: You mean this one; right? Or this? This is -- what should I call it? These were shops. This was a candy shop or an ice-cream parlor right here. This is where the health centre was, and this other one is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you again mark a circle where you say the candy shop was.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And please add the letter G next to it.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. And just my last question. Are there any other important buildings on this photo which you think we should know about?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. You see this one over here, the yellow one, this was the locally commune building, and that's what it was during the war as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. You just circled it. Please add the letter H next to it.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: I put a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Thank you very much, Mr. Luinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That concludes my examination-in-chief, Mr. President. And I would like to tender this photo into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P299, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we have five minutes for cross-examination. Didn't you say you were finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was thinking. I'm sorry, I'm sitting down right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I represent Dragomir Milosevic. Not only because it's my duty but because I fell a general need, I would like to ask you something about some of your answers that you provided in chief. Please be as brief as you can.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The first thing I heard is you were a reserve police officer throughout the war; right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war you were armed, armed as you described, a rifle and a pistol; right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You never used either of these weapons, did you, to fire?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: I had a licenced pistol from before the war. Back at home where I lived, and I lived near the airport, in Akifa Seremeta 14, the Aerodrom neighbourhood, that's where I had my flat --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you keep it brief, please.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs came along and they took my pistol away, the licenced gun that I had, and I never saw it again. It was never given back to me. The pistol that I had was one that I'd signed for back at the station. They gave it to me. I didn't actually make anyone issue me with a gun. Being a police officer, I was probably supposed to carry a weapon. In town you need a weapon; you can't just walk around like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At some point during the war, probably, your hand was forced. You had to use your weapon, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: I worked with civilians. That sort of thing was not called for, believe me. But I just carried it around.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to focus in my cross-examination - and I mean that about tomorrow, too - on the time-period between the 10th of August and November, around that time when the Dayton Accords were signed. I want to know about that time-period and that's what I'll be asking you about.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout this period, was there any firing at all from Sarajevo? Perhaps you can tell me about that. Perhaps you can tell me about what the citizens of Sarajevo experienced throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: You just watched it on TV, I suppose, didn't you? There were all sorts of things happening; people being killed, people being wounded, hungry people. Most of all, hungry people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about across the front line?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, across the front line? Who was firing; is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, what I'm asking you is was there any firing from inside Sarajevo, firing across the front line, the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: I'll answer like this. I was no commander or anything. I was just a salt-of-the-earth police officer. I didn't have any business being at the front line, firing bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But that wasn't my question, was it?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Fine, fine. I'm just telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I was asking if anyone in Sarajevo was firing at the Serbs, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I just said it, haven't I? I was no commander. I didn't order anyone to fire. I carried this rifle, but someone else actually cleaned it for me, because it was raining very often and the rifle had begun to rust, the iron bits did. So I can't answer that question, can I?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that nobody from Sarajevo ever fired at the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: I haven't a clue, to be quite frank.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A while ago, in answer to one of the questions by the Prosecutor, you said that in this area you never saw any heavy weapons or a mortar. Nothing like that.

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: I would be the first to stand up against it. There was never anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Stand up against it? What exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: DZEMALUDIN LUINOVIC
utterances.text: I told him them to go away. I'd do anything I could. I want my child to be left in peace. Let me tell you something. The Serb army had all sorts of weapons, heavy weapons. They were in a position to detect where fire was coming from, you know. They were in a position to say. And sometimes they would ascertain that fire was coming from a particular neighbourhood, and obviously they would just shower the place with shells.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to break for the day and resume tomorrow at 2.15 p.m.
